Fifteen thousand people, each handed a flag or a bandanna on a stick. The Sun: "The hands of the watches of those who were timing the tumult measured 41 minutes and 30 seconds. It was only quelled at last by those who insisted that the Colonel should be allowed to speak."

He made no effort to use his right hand at all.

Sixteen days after he was shot in Milwaukee, Theodore Roosevelt came back to the stump at Madison Square Garden.

The Sun put four in ten of the crowd women, and its police source reckoned it the biggest throng at that hall since Bryan spoke there in 1896. Edith Roosevelt came in only when it was almost time for her husband to speak, and passed unnoticed to a box directly across from the platform.

Each person had a flag or a bandanna on a stick. He waved his left arm at fifteen thousand people, they jumped to their feet, and from the platform the crowd "seemed to be overswept with a flaming wave of red."

Then they cheered, and would not stop.

"The hands of the watches of those who were timing the tumult measured 41 minutes and 30 seconds. It was only quelled at last by those who insisted that the Colonel should be allowed to speak."

He was still hurt, and it showed while the noise went on. His face was "gleaming with perspiration" and his jaws were snapping. He made no effort to use his right hand at all.

He finished: "I believe we shall win, but win or lose I am glad beyond measure that I am one of the many who in this fight have stood ready to spend and be spent."

He lost. The next night Woodrow Wilson made his last New York speech of the campaign in the same building.

Sixteen days after he was shot in Milwaukee, Theodore Roosevelt came back to the stump at Madison Square Garden.

People had been arriving since the afternoon. The Sun put four in ten of the crowd women, and its police source reckoned it the biggest throng at that hall since Bryan spoke there in 1896. In the boxes were "men and women dressed as for the opera." Edith Roosevelt did not come in until it was almost time for her husband to speak, then passed unnoticed to a box directly across from the platform and sat there smiling while the hall cheered for him.

Each person had been handed a flag or a bandanna on a stick. He came forward and waved his left arm at fifteen thousand people, they jumped to their feet, and from the platform the crowd "seemed to be overswept with a flaming wave of red."

Then they cheered, and would not stop.

"The hands of the watches of those who were timing the tumult measured 41 minutes and 30 seconds. It was only quelled at last by those who insisted that the Colonel should be allowed to speak."

Not a round number. Forty-one minutes and thirty seconds, by the watches of the men timing it.

He was still hurt, and it showed while the noise went on. By the end of half an hour his face was "gleaming with perspiration" and his jaws were snapping, the Sun wrote, "as though he were bent upon keeping himself in trim for the speech." He made no effort to use his right hand at all. He raised his left and extended it over the audience, asking them to give him a hearing.

He closed by reading back a passage of his own from earlier in the campaign, and then:

"Friends, what I said then I say now. Surely there never was a greater opportunity than ours. Surely there never was a fight better worth making than this. I believe we shall win, but win or lose I am glad beyond measure that I am one of the many who in this fight have stood ready to spend and be spent, pledged to fight while life lasts the great fight for righteousness and for brotherhood and for the welfare of mankind."

He lost. The following night, Woodrow Wilson made his last New York speech of the campaign in the same building.

#OTD 31 October 1879. TR, 21, spent the day shooting, then went to "a very pleasant "All-Hallow E'en" party at the Swans, where we had great fun, going through the canonical rites and dancing besides."

He doesn't say which rites.

Friday, 31 October 1879. Theodore Roosevelt was twenty-one — he had turned twenty-one on the Monday — and home at Oyster Bay, away from Harvard in the middle of his senior year.

He spent the day shooting. From his diary, in his own hand:

"Took an old gunner, "Ramson", and drove off to an old farm house about eight miles off; spent six or seven hours walking through the woods and stubble fields. The quail were plenty; but scattered easily and had to be whistled together."

At the foot of the page, the tally he kept on shooting days: 3 rabbit, 3 woodcock, 9 quail.

Then he washed up and went to a party.

"In the evening went to a very pleasant "All-Hallow E'en" party at the Swans, where we had great fun, going through the canonical rites and dancing besides."

The canonical rites. A twenty-one-year-old treating a parlour game as liturgy — and then, maddeningly, not saying which ones.

So all anyone can say is what was in the air. An 1879 Halloween was a fortune-telling night, and most of the fortunes were about who you were going to marry. An Ohio paper printing that same weekend ran through the old repertoire: molten lead poured through the wards of a key into water, an apple paring thrown over the left shoulder to land in the shape of an initial, chestnuts set out in pairs. It also observed that the customs varied from one country to another and even between parts of the same country — and thought the rites were dying out anyway, leaving mostly the pranks of youngsters and the carrying-off of gates.

Chambers's Book of Days, the standard Victorian catalogue of such things, runs through the British and Irish versions: ducking for apples in a tub of water; nuts named for sweethearts set on the grate, to see whether they burn quietly side by side or jump apart; and, in Scotland, a kail-stalk pulled up blindfold in a dark garden and read for the shape of a future spouse.

He went through them. He doesn't say which.

What the entry does not mention is who had been on his mind that autumn. Nine days earlier he and a friend had given an opera party, and the diary lists the guests — among them "Rose and Alice." Two days after the Swans' party he went into New York and called on the Lees.

He married Alice Hathaway Lee a year later, on his twenty-second birthday.

He lost, and he lost badly.

On 2 November 1886 New York City elected Abram S. Hewitt mayor. Henry George, the single-tax reformer, came second. Theodore Roosevelt, twenty-eight years old and the Republican candidate, came third. The official canvass, declared eleven days later: Hewitt 90,552, George 68,110, Roosevelt 60,435.

The Tribune's front page the next morning is worth looking at, because it does not shout. Six columns of solid grey type and no display headline anywhere on the page. The result sits in a single column at the far right, in letters about a sixth of an inch high: HEWITT THE NEXT MAYOR. Underneath, smaller again: GEORGE RUNS AHEAD OF ROOSEVELT.

Roosevelt wired Henry Cabot Lodge in Boston, who had just won his seat in Congress by 728 votes. This is the whole telegram:

"Am more delighted than I can say. Do come on Thursday.
Am badly defeated. Worse even than I feared."

Note the order. The first line is about his friend. His own defeat comes second, in eight words, with no explanation and no excuse attached to it.

Lodge went straight to him. He wrote later:

"I went on immediately after this telegram was received and was with him and his sister until they sailed for Europe a day or two later. Roosevelt had made a fine and very telling campaign and was in excellent spirits in all ways and very happy in his approaching marriage."

"Am going to give an accurate abstract of my doings this week, as a sampl."

Then, down the page in his own hand:

7.45 prayers   8.00 breakfast.
8.30 – 1.00 study. 1.00 lunch.
1.30 – 4.30 study. 4.30 – 6.00 walk.
7.00 went to dinner to University Crew.
Came out towards 12.00 and lounged in Club for a couple of hours.

The Club is almost certainly the Porcellian, into which he had been initiated on the Saturday — and which had cost him the Sunday: "Rather under the weather, owing to last nights spree."

Tuesday begins the same way and is then interrupted. "To my utter astonishment Nell & Mother turned up, on for the day." His brother Elliott and his mother, unannounced. Wednesday holds: studied 8.30 to 4.00, then a walk with Dick Saltonstall and Jack Tebbetts.

He struck out what he had written on the page headed Thursday, drew two diagonal strokes across it, and wrote the real Thursday entry on the next leaf — crossing out the printed "FRIDAY 8" and writing "Thursday" above it. Then he re-dated the next four pages by hand, until the diary caught up with itself.

The accurate abstract survived all of that. Friday: "Studied 9.00 – 5.30. In the evening had a supper, with 8 or ten of the fellows, in the club — partridges & burgundy. Did not get to bed till towards two a.m."

By Saturday he had stopped keeping the log.

From June 1902 the Roosevelts did not live in the White House. Charles McKim had gutted it.

On 5 November they came back. The President stopped in Philadelphia to speak on the way; he and Edith and the two youngest boys, Archie and Quentin, reached Washington at twenty past seven that evening and slept in the house for the first time since the summer. He was at his desk in the new offices west of the house by half past nine the next morning.

The Evening Star, reporting it, put the state of the place carefully: "The improvements throughout the building are still incomplete, but there is sufficient completed space for the accommodation of the household for the present."

Which is a generous way of saying the lower floor was still a building site. He left again for New York the following Monday.

The room that had changed most was the State Dining Room. McKim had pulled out the grand staircase and pushed the room into its footprint, making a room that could seat more than a hundred.

That sharpened a problem the house had been quietly carrying for a century. An inventory made the year before, under McKinley, had found very little china left from previous administrations — certainly nothing that would set a table for a hundred.

What Edith Roosevelt did about that is why there is a White House china collection. She ordered a Wedgwood service of 1,344 pieces. She had cabinets built in the ground-floor corridor where visitors could see the older china. She ruled that nothing be bought — only given or lent. She had the collection made official government property so that it could never be dispersed. And she directed that broken pieces be destroyed rather than sold at auction — TR's military aide Archie Butt wrote that she thought that method "cheapens the White House."

The idea was not originally hers. Caroline Harrison had wanted a cabinet built for the china a decade earlier and died before it happened. But the collection is Edith's doing, and it begins in a house still too full of builders' dust to lay a table properly.

The Cunard liner Etruria was advertised to leave Pier 40, North River, at one o'clock on Saturday 6 November 1886. Mails closed at ten. Cabin passage was $60, $80 and $100.

Four days after losing the New York mayoral election, Theodore Roosevelt went aboard her. The Times listed the party the next morning — "Mr. and Mrs. Douglas Robinson, Miss Roosevelt, and Mr. Theodore Roosevelt" — his sister Corinne and her husband, his sister Bamie, and him. They were going over for his wedding.

Somewhere on the same ship was a young British diplomat named Cecil Spring Rice. He had been told in advance that the Roosevelts would be aboard and that he should go and introduce himself. He did.

Writing home about the crossing, Spring Rice described his new acquaintance:

"I came over with Roosevelt, who has been standing for the mayoralty of New York against H. George and who is supposed to be the boss Republican young man. He is going to be married and then to be in England in February so that you will see him, I hope."

Twenty-six days later, Spring Rice was best man at the wedding.

The Etruria was not the only ship due out of the North River at one o'clock that afternoon. The French liner La Gascogne was leaving at the same hour, carrying Ferdinand de Lesseps and part of the French delegation home from the unveiling of the Statue of Liberty nine days earlier. The Etruria took the lead, and La Gascogne, in the Times' phrase, "quietly waited until she was well under way before she followed her."

The Sun put the sailing on its front page the next morning. He was, it said, "accompanied to the steamer by many of his family and friends and sent off with warm wishes and congratulations."

A week later, at twenty to twelve on the morning of Saturday 13 November, the Etruria reached Queenstown.

Eleven days married. Theodore Roosevelt's diary for Sunday 7 November 1880, in his own hand — this is the whole entry:

"In the morning I read aloud from the bible; in the afternoon we took a long walk through woods and fields, in the beautiful, clear, cool Autumn weather. Alice is a beautiful walker, with her long, firm step, and clambers over fences about as easily as I do.

My old hunter keeps us pretty well supplied with woodcock & partridge."

It is the second sentence that does the work. A twenty-two-year-old noting, apparently with pleasure, that his wife can keep up with him and get over a fence as easily as he can.

The day before, rain had kept them indoors: "I love to talk over everything with Baby, from Politics to Poetry, and to read aloud to her, either from a History or standard novel or from the daily newspaper that forms our only intercourse with the outside world."

Armistice Day, 11 November 1918. At 11 a.m. the guns fell silent on the Western Front.

That same Monday, Theodore Roosevelt went back into Roosevelt Hospital in New York City, in severe pain.

All four of his sons had gone to war. Archie and Ted had been wounded. Quentin, the youngest, a pilot, had been shot down and killed over France that July. He was 20.

For most of the next six weeks, Edith Roosevelt lived at the hospital, in a room next to her husband's. He came home to Sagamore Hill at Christmas. He died there in his sleep on 6 January 1919, at 60.

On Monday 13 November 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt had a houseguest he admired: Frederick Courteney Selous, the British hunter and explorer. Selous had spent decades in southern Africa, a career that included guiding Cecil Rhodes's 1890 expedition into what became Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe.

"He is a perfect old dear; just as simple and natural as can be and very interesting," Roosevelt wrote to his son Kermit a few days later.

In the afternoon Roosevelt took him "for a good scramble and climb" with a party that included Gifford Pinchot. Before dinner, he wrote, he got Selous "to spend three-quarters of an hour in telling delightfully exciting lion and hyena stories to Ethel, Archie and Quentin."

https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/legacy/teddy-bear

The real story behind the teddy bear is rougher than the toy.

On 14 November 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt was on a bear hunt in the Mississippi Delta, near Smedes. His guide was Holt Collier, born enslaved and by then a renowned bear hunter in the Delta. Roosevelt later wrote that Collier had spent half a century hunting bears, "having killed or assisted in killing over three thousand bears."

The president had no luck that day. While he was back at camp for lunch, Collier's hounds ran a bear into a water hole. The exhausted animal killed one of the dogs. Collier struck it with his rifle and sent word for Roosevelt. Meanwhile he roped the bear and tied it to a tree.

Roosevelt arrived to find a stunned, bloodied bear tied up and waiting for him. He refused to shoot it. He had it put out of its misery instead, and it was killed with a knife.

He was not pleased. Writing to a friend later that month, he called it "a most unsatisfactory experience in a bear hunt in Mississippi," and said his hosts had turned the outing into "a cross between a hunt and a picnic."

The newspapers saw it differently. Clifford Berryman drew the scene for the front page of The Washington Post, captioned "Drawing the Line in Mississippi." In the cartoon the bear looks like a cub. The real one, newspapers reported, was a grown bear of more than 200 pounds.

In Brooklyn, shopkeepers Morris and Rose Michtom made a stuffed bear; family accounts say they called it "Teddy's bear." Within a few years, toy bears were a national craze.

Holt Collier has his own legacy. The Holt Collier National Wildlife Refuge in the Mississippi Delta bears his name; the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service calls it the only national wildlife refuge named for an African American.

On 14 November 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt was on a bear hunt in the Mississippi Delta, near Smedes. His guide was Holt Collier, born enslaved and by then a renowned bear hunter in the Delta. Roosevelt later wrote that Collier had spent half a century hunting bears, "having killed or assisted in killing over three thousand bears."

The president had no luck that day. While he was back at camp for lunch, Collier's hounds ran a bear into a water hole. The exhausted animal killed one of the dogs. Collier struck it with his rifle and sent word for Roosevelt. Meanwhile he roped the bear and tied it to a tree.

Roosevelt arrived to find a stunned, bloodied bear tied up and waiting for him. He refused to shoot it. He had it put out of its misery instead, and it was killed with a knife.

He was not pleased. Writing to a friend later that month, he called it "a most unsatisfactory experience in a bear hunt in Mississippi," and said his hosts had turned the outing into "a cross between a hunt and a picnic."

The newspapers saw it differently. Clifford Berryman drew the scene for the front page of The Washington Post, captioned "Drawing the Line in Mississippi." In the cartoon the bear looks like a cub. The real one, newspapers reported, was a grown bear of more than 200 pounds.

In Brooklyn, shopkeepers Morris and Rose Michtom made a stuffed bear; family accounts say they called it "Teddy's bear." Within a few years, toy bears were a national craze.

Holt Collier has his own legacy. The Holt Collier National Wildlife Refuge in the Mississippi Delta bears his name; the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service calls it the only national wildlife refuge named for an African American.

#OTD 15 November 1906. 120 years ago, Theodore Roosevelt comes ashore in Panama to inspect the canal: the first visit abroad by a sitting president.

He chose November "partly because it is the rainiest month of the year," and it rained for three days.

120 years ago today, a president of the United States stepped ashore in a foreign country to see a job for himself.

The battleship Louisiana reached Colón, Panama, a day early, on the afternoon of Wednesday 14 November 1906. On Thursday morning, 15 November, Theodore Roosevelt came ashore to inspect the Panama Canal. The State Department records the trip as the first visit abroad by a sitting president. The Canal Zone had come under American control after Panama broke away from Colombia in 1903, with American support.

He picked the season on purpose. "I chose the month of November for my visit partly because it is the rainiest month of the year, the month in which the work goes forward at the greatest disadvantage, and one of the two months which the medical department of the French Canal Company found most unhealthy," he told Congress afterward.

It was raining when he came ashore, and the rain hardly let up for three days.

That first day, by his own report, he toured the bay by tug, inspected Ancon Hospital, and dropped in for a meal without notice. "I myself took dinner at the La Boca government hotel, no warning whatever having been given of my coming," he wrote. His meal, he said, was "excellent." The 30-cent meal at those hotels ran to soup, beef, mashed potatoes, peas, beets, chili con carne and plum pudding.

Those hotels served the canal's white American employees. Most of the canal's labor force, tens of thousands of workers, came from the West Indies, and they were paid and housed separately.

The next morning he climbed into the cab of one of the 95-ton steam shovels as the rain came on, and that photograph is shown here too.
